tooltip.title: Classification of Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: A systematic breakdown of the major categories and specific types of hair loss.

tooltip.title: Non-Scarring (Noncicatricial) Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: A group of alopecias where the hair follicle is preserved, and hair regrowth is possible. Characterized by the presence of follicular ostia on exam.

tooltip.title: Androgenetic Alopecia (AGA)
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Pathophysiology:** Genetically determined, androgen-mediated progressive miniaturization of hair follicles.
-   **Presentation:** Male Pattern Hair Loss (MPHL) and Female Pattern Hair Loss (FPHL).

tooltip.title: Alopecia Areata (AA)
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Pathophysiology:** Autoimmune attack on the anagen hair bulb, leading to rapid, patchy hair loss.
-   **Variants:** Can be patchy, totalis (all scalp hair), or universalis (all body hair).

tooltip.title: Telogen Effluvium (TE)
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Pathophysiology:** An abrupt shift of a large number of hairs from the anagen (growth) phase to the telogen (resting) phase, leading to diffuse shedding ~3 months later.
-   **Triggers:** Illness, surgery, childbirth, stress, medications.

tooltip.title: Anagen Effluvium
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Pathophysiology:** An insult that abruptly stops mitotic activity in the anagen hair bulb, causing the shaft to break and shed rapidly.
-   **Primary Cause:** Chemotherapy.

tooltip.title: Traumatic/Mechanical Alopecias
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Traction Alopecia:** Hair loss from prolonged or repetitive tension on the hair follicle. Can become scarring if chronic.
-   **Trichotillomania:** An impulse-control disorder characterized by the compulsive pulling out of hair.

tooltip.title: Scarring (Cicatricial) Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: A group of inflammatory disorders that cause permanent destruction of the hair follicle, leading to irreversible hair loss. Characterized by loss of follicular ostia.

tooltip.title: Primary Lymphocytic Cicatricial Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: The inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of lymphocytes.

tooltip.title: Lichen Planopilaris (LPP)
tooltip.markdown: Presents with perifollicular erythema and scale, typically on the vertex scalp.

tooltip.title: Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia (FFA)
tooltip.markdown: A variant of LPP causing a progressive band of alopecia along the frontal hairline.

tooltip.title: Central Centrifugal Cicatricial Alopecia (CCCA)
tooltip.markdown: Begins on the crown and spreads centrifugally. Most common in women of African descent.

tooltip.title: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE)
tooltip.markdown: Presents as erythematous, atrophic plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugging.

tooltip.title: Primary Neutrophilic Cicatricial Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: The inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of neutrophils.

tooltip.title: Folliculitis Decalvans (FD)
tooltip.markdown: Characterized by chronic pustules, erosions, and crusting, often leading to hair tufting.

tooltip.title: Dissecting Cellulitis of the Scalp (DC)
tooltip.markdown: Presents as painful, boggy nodules and abscesses that interconnect, forming sinus tracts.

tooltip.title: Medication-Induced Alopecias
tooltip.markdown: Hair loss as a direct adverse effect of a medication. Can manifest as various types of alopecia.

tooltip.title: Telogen Effluvium Inducers
tooltip.markdown: The most common form of drug-induced hair loss. Examples include retinoids, beta-blockers, anticoagulants.

tooltip.title: Anagen Effluvium Inducers
tooltip.markdown: Primarily caused by cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents.

tooltip.title: Alopecia Areata Inducers
tooltip.markdown: Less common, but can be paradoxically induced by biologics like TNF-alpha inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
